lawyer:
Mr. Md. Zahirul Islam Mukul, Advocate ----- for the appellant. 
Mr. Md. Delwar Hossain, Advocate ----- for the respondents.
parties:
Albert Subir Biswas ------- Appellant
Vs.
Abdur Rab Rashidi & Babul Rashid and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Sikder Maqbul Huq, J: This First Misc. Appeal is directed against the order dated 17.1.99 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court Dhaka disallowing Misc. Case No. 17 of 1996 for violation of the order of the Court. 

 4. It has been alleged by the petitioner that even in face of the order of status quo defendant opposite party No. 1 continued to threaten the plaintiff-petitioner and the members of his family to dispossess him from the suit property. In such circumstances, the plaintiff-petitioner made a G.D. entry at the Gulshan P.S. on 12.4.95. The plaintiff further lodged, by registered post, a G.D. entry with the O.C. of Gulshan P.S. on 30.7.95 stating that opposite party No. 1 and his companion miscreants were constantly threatening to forcibly enter into the suit premises for dispossessing the plaintiff and the members of his family from the suit premises. Opposite party No. 1 and his men even threatened to kill the petitioner along with the members of his family and to destroy his entire property if the failed to vacate the suit premises by the given time. In such ominous circumstances, the petitioner on 15.3.96 tiled a case at Gulshan P.S. for vindication of his grievances but the Gulshan P. S. for unknown reasons made a G.D. entry instead of starting a regular criminal case. The plaintiff petitioner then filed a case in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, on 9.3.96 against persons named in the G.D. entry, including opposite party No. 1. The learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, referred the matter to the Officer-in-Charge Gulshan P.S. for treating it as FIR. on 19th March, 96 opposite party No. 1 and his associates being armed with deadly weapons forcibly entered into the suit premises and looted away furniture, valuable timber and other valuable goods and thereafter forcibly evicted the petitioner and other members of his family therefrom on 19.3.96 and thereby willfully violated the order of status quo granted by the Court. They also assaulted the members of the family of the petitioner and his workers and as such they should be punished by detention in civil prison for violating the order of restraint passed by the Court. 

 5. The opposite parties resisted the Misc. Case by filing a joint written objection denying the material allegations of the petitioner and contended inter alia that the plaintiff petitioner was a tenant under defendant No. 1 in respect of the suit premises but he failed to pay monthly rent from October, 1994 to the May, 95 and as such on 2.6.95 defendant opposite party No. 1 convened a salish in presence of the local influential persons namely Abul Flashem, Feroz Ahmed, Md. Hossain Khan and others. In that salish the plaintiff petitioner admitted that he could not pay rent for the aforesaid months. It was agreed in that salish that the plaintiff petitioner would pay the arrear monthly rent amounting to Tk. 44,000.00, including rent for the month June, 1995 within the month of July, 1995, failing which he would vacate the suit premises by 31th July, 1995. The plaintiff petitioner could not pay the arrear rent of Tk. 44,000.00 within the month of July, 1995 and as such a second salish was convened with the local influential persons and at the mediation of the salishdars the petitioner handed over possession of the suit premises to opposite party No. 1 on 10-11/8/95 and went away with his belongings. It has also been alleged that the opposite parties never violated the order of status quo passed by the Court. It has also been alleged that the plaintiff petitioner has been harassing them by tiling false civil and criminal cases with oblique motives. 

 6. At the trial the contending parties examined 5 witnesses each and exhibited documents in support of their respective cases. 

 7. The learned Subordinate Judge by his impugned order dated 17.1.99 disallowed the Misc. case on the finding that the petitioner could not prove his case beyond reasonable doubts by adducing reliable evidences. 

 9. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed a clear error of law and facts in disallowing the Misc. case in the face of the most cogent and corroborative evidence of 5 PWs. who convincingly proved beyond any reasonable doubt that opposite party No. 1, with his men, willfully violated the order of status quo passed by the learned Subordinate Judge by forcibly entering into the suit premises and by evicting the plaintiff petitioner and the members of his family therefrom on 19.3.96 and looting away his valuable goods worth Tk. 30 lacs. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in not discarding the defence plea that the plaintiff petitioner voluntarily vacated the suit premises on the ground that opposite party No. 1 never took such a plea in his written objection against the application for temporary injunction tiled long after the illegal and forcible eviction of the plaintiff petitioner by opposite party No. 1 from the suit premises; Even in his written objection filed by opposite party No. 1 against the application for violation of the order of status quo, he did not mention the date and the precise time for the alleged voluntary vacation of the suit premises by the petitioner on 10-11/8/95. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the opposite parties filed written objection in the case on 24.8.95 but it was completely silent about vacating the suit premises voluntarily by the plaintiff petitioner or his entering upon the same on 10-11.8.95 or on any other date on vacation of possession voluntarily by the plaintiff petitioner. The learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider this vital aspect of the case thereby fell in error in passing the impugned order on misreading and non-reading of the material evidence and non-consideration of vital facts and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant petitioner also submits that out of the 5 witnesses examined by the opposite parties, 3(three) are opposite parties themselves in the case, who admittedly are instrumental in compelling the petitioner and the members of his family in vacating the suit premises and who themselves looted away valuable properties of the petitioner but the learned Subordinate Judge on a misreading of this material evidence and vital fact found that the witness examined by the defendant are disinterested persons and made it a ground for the impugned decision. The learned Advocate for the appellant petitioner lastly submits that regard being had to the fact that plaintiff-petitioner has proved the willful violation of the order of status quo by most consistent, corroborative and overwhelming evidence, both oral and documentary, the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in not punishing the opposite parties on illegal and irrelevant considerations occasioning failure of justice. 

 10. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondents submits that this being a case of quasi criminal nature, the plaintiff petitioner is required to prove his case reasonable doubts and unless it is done, the case is liable to be disallowed, even if the opposite parties adduced no evidence in support of their plea. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in disallowing the Misc. case in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record. 

 Let us now consider the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides in the light of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 13. P.W. 1, Albert Subir Biswas is the petitioner in the case. He stales in his evidence that the order of status quo was passed in Title Suit No. 161 of 1995 on 30.7.95 and the same was made absolute on 28.10.95 after hearing both sides. He further states that he was in possession of the entire premises from before the said order of status quo. He Further says that on 10.3.96 opposite parties Siraj Matin and another entered into the suit premises and asked him as to why he did not see opposite party Quayum although he was asked to do so, and directed him to meet opposite party Quayum forthwith for discussions regarding the disputed property whereupon he replied that he would not go to see him unless notice was given. It is also in his deposition that on 15.3.96 at about 4.30 P.M. while he was going to Gulshan P.S. for lodging a complaint. opposite parties Harun, Abdur Rob, Quayum, Mann and their associates forcibly entered into the suit premises and looted away valuable goods and threatened him with murder in case of his failure to vacate the suit premises within 24 hours. On the same day he made a G.D. entry to these effects with O.C. Gulshan P.S. and thereafter he made another G.D. Entry on 19.3.1996 at about 3.00 P.M. He further stated that later Harun, accompanied by 4/5 persons came to the suit premises and threatened the members of his family and on the same day at about 4.30 P.M. the opposite parties forcibly entered into the suit premises and looted away valuable goods of the petitioner. It is also in his evidence that the opposite parties looted away his properties worth Tk. 30 lacs as described in schedule of the properties to the application of the Misc. Case. He further says that he used to live in the suit premises with members of his family and in one side of the sun house he used to run a furniture making factory. He also states in his evidence that a portion of the looted properties was subsequently recovered by the police from Dholaikhal area of the Dhaka City on preparing a seizure list Ext. 1. He went on to state that after proper investigation the police submitted charge sheet, ext. 2, in the case against the accused persons. He strongly refuted the defence suggestion that he had voluntarily vacated the suit premises on 10-11/8/95. He also stated that he entered into the suit premises in 1982 as a monthly tenant at a monthly rent of Tk. 650.00 and denied any subsequent increment of rent. He also denies the suggestion that he had agreed either pay to pay the arrear rent of Tk. 44000.00 by the month of July 95 or to vacate the suit premises. He denied the suggestion that he had no property worth Tk. 30 lac or that he could not pay the arrear rent or that the opposite parties did not dispossess him forcibly from the suit property. He further says in his cross-examination that he did not file any case in the Gulshan P.S. regarding the alleged dispossession and looting away of valuable goods as the Gulshan P.S. did not take any action on the occurrence that took place on 18.3.96. He further says that he informed the Gulshan P.S. about the occurrence 014th of April but no action has been taken by the police. It is also in his evidence that owners of the adjoining shops and his neighbours do not care come to depose in the case as the opposite parties are dangerous terrorists. Evidences on record tends to show that opposite party No. 1 and his associates are dangerous and desperate by nature. 

 16. P.W. 4 Richard Biswas has fully corroborated the case of the petitioner in all material particulars. He has stated in details the goods, including the furniture and machinery, taken away by the opposite parties from the possession of the petitioner. He empathically denied the defence suggestion that P.W. 1 voluntarily vacated the suit premises as he could not pay the arrear rent amounting to Tk. 44,000.00. His evidence could not at all be shaken in cross-examination. It appears that he is distantly related to P.W.1 and he used to work in his work in his workshop but this cannot be a ground to disbelieve him as he is found to be a natural, probable and truthful witness. 

 17. P.W. 5 Albert Rorbert Biswas was in the suit premises on the date of the forcible eviction of the petitioner by the opposite parties in violation of the status quo order lie fully corroborated the evidence of P.Ws. 1-2 regarding the forcible dispossession of the petitioner by the opposite parties from the suit property on the fateful day. He clearly stated that they could not resist the opposite parties as they were armed with deadly weapons. It may, in this connection, be mentioned that other witnesses also stated in their evidence that the opposite parties had arms with them at the time of the occurrence. This witness, it appears, was also an employee of P.W. 1 and he also used to work in the furniture factory of P.W. 1 in the suit premises. He emphatically denies the suggestion that P.W. 1 voluntarily vacated the suit premises as he could not pay the arrear rent. The defence miserably failed to discredit his evidence in any way whatsoever. There is no reason on his part to depose falsely in the case. He is found to be a natural and truthful witness. 

 18. Opposite party No. 1 Abdur Rab Rashidi is the principal defendant in the suit for specific performance of contract. He states in his evidence that P.W. 1 was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises under him. He also says that initially monthly rent of the suit premises was Tk. 650.00, which was ultimately raised to Tk. 5,500.00. He further asserts that he had a written agreement to that effect but no agreement could be produced in the Court. He stated that P.W. I failed to pay the rent from October, 1994 and as such there was a salish over the matter on 2.6.95 in presence of the other opposite parties wherein it was decided that the petitioner would either pay the arrear rent of Tk. 44,000.00 or vacate the suit premises within 2 months but he did not pay the arrear rent by 31.7.95 and as such there was another salish in the month of August. In that salish it was settled that the petitioners would clear up the arrear rent and vacate the suit premises but did he not pay the rent. It may, in this connection, be mentioned that the opposite parties had no case in his written objection filed about 151 days of the forcible dispossession that it was decided in the said 2nd salish that the petitioner would pay up the arrear rent and vacate the premises. It was totally absent in the said written objection that the petitioner voluntarily vacated the suit property in favour of opposite party No. 1. Even in his written objection filed after about 10 (ten) months of the date of forcible dispossession on 19.3.1996 opposite party No. 1 made some vague statements regarding the vacating of the suit premises by the petitioner but he failed to give the date and time of the alleged surrender. This witness denied to have assaulted the inmates of the suit premises as alleged. During cross-examination, he stated that he went into possession of the suit premises on 10-11/8/95. He admitted during his cross-examination that the order of status quo was passed on 30.7.1995 and he further admitted that P.W.1 was in possession of the suit premises at the time of salish on 7.8.95. He further states that the decisions in the salish were not reduced to writing. He denied that he willfully violated the status quo order. 

 19. O.P.W. 2 M.A. Quayum is O.P. 2 in the violation Misc. Case. He states that on 7.8.95 there was a salish in presence of the opposite parties regarding the suit premises in which it was settled that the tenant would leave the suit premises after clearing the arrear rent within 48 hours. He also stated that P.W. i was given 48 hours’ time to vacate the suit premises which clearly indicates that P.W. I was forced to leave the suit premises at the instance of the opposite parties. He further stated that P.W. 1 thereafter vacated the suit premises and he heard it from O.P.W. 1 but O.P.W. I did not state in his evidence that he told O.P.W. 2 M.A. Quayum or any other witness about voluntary surrender of the suit premises by the petitioner on the alleged date of the occurrence. This statement of O.P.W. No. 2 on this point is thus legally inadmissible in evidence. 

 21. 0. P.W. 3 Md. Serajul Islam is O.P. No. 5 in this case. He states that P.W. 1 was a tenant in respect of the disputed premises under opposite party No. 1. He further says that the first salish over rent dispute was held on 2.6.95 and the petitioner was allowed time upto 31.7.95 to pay the arrears rent but the petitioner did not abide by this decision and did not pay the rent by the given time and the second salish was held in which the petitioner was given 48 hours’ time to clear up the arrear rent. During cross-examination, he stated that he is not aware of the suit or of the order of status quo in respect of the disputed premises. He, however, denied to have forcibly entered into the suit premises and evicted the petitioner therefrom or to have looted away his properties. 

 22. O.P.W. 4 Abul Hashem stated in his evidence that it had been decided in the first salsih that the petitioner would vacate the suit premises within 2 months and that in the 2nd salish the petitioner was allowed only two days' time to vacate the premise's and to pay the arrear rent. During cross-examination, he stated that the petitioner had a furniture factory by the side of his (petitioner) dwelling house. This statement of O.P.W. 4 lends support to the case of the petitioner that he used to run a factory in a part of the suit premises. He has also denied the suggestion regarding forcible eviction, looting and violation of the status quo order. 

 24. No other witness has been examined in this case. 

 25. In this case certain facts stand admitted. There is no dispute about the fact that the petitioner had been a tenant in respect of the suit premises since 1982 under the predecessor-in-interest of the O.P.W. No. 1 and subsequently under him after O.P.W.1 got the property by inheritance and gift. There is also no dispute about the fact that the petitioner has earlier instituted Title Suit No. 161 of 1995 in the Court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka for specific performance of the contract in respect the suit property against O.P.W. 1 and others stating that O.P. 1 entered into a contract to sell the suit property to the petitioner on the basis of a bainapatra for a consideration of Tk. 9 lacs out of which Tk. 8 lacs has already been paid to the contesting defendant as earnest money. There is also no dispute about the fact that the petitioner after institution of the suit, prayed for an order of temporary injunction on 25.7.95 and subsequently an ex-parte order restraining the opposite party No. 1 from entering into the suit premises and interfering with the possession of the petitioner therein was passed where after the opposite party No. 1 tiled a written objection. Subsequently the learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties by his order dated 28.10.95 directed the parties to maintain status quo in respect or possession in the suit property and the said order of status quo is still in full force. It is in evidence that before and alter the order of status quo was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge the petitioner made several G.D entries and also tiled a criminal case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. Dhaka alleging that opposite party No. 1. and his men were continuously threatening him and the members of his family with dispossession from the suit premises. There was even allegation of threat of murder of the petitioner by opposite party No.1 Opposite party No. I tiled written objection against the prayer for injunction on 24.8.95. at least 10(ten) days after the order of status quo was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge on hearing the contending parties but in the said written objection he did not at all mention that he went into possession in the suit premises on 10-11/8/95 after the same was voluntarily vacated by petitioner Albert Subir Biswas. It is also found from the record that opposite party No. 1 never brought this vital fact to the notice of the learned Subordinate Judge at any point of time that the petitioner had voluntarily vacated the suit premises following which he went into possession of the suit property. Had the petitioner vacated the suit premises voluntarily or had opposite party No. 1 taken over the possession thereof on 10-11/8/95 following the surrender, there is no earthly reason for him for not mentioning this vital tact in his written objection filed by him on 24.8.95 against the prayer for temporary injunction or for bringing this vital fact to the notice of the Court during the hearing of the injunction matter or at any point of time. Opposite party No. I did not even specifically mention in his written objection tiled in the Misc. Case that he went into possession of the suit premises on 10-11/8/95 after the plaintiff petitioner had voluntarily vacated the suit premises in his favour. Except making some vague assertions about vacating the suit property by the petitioner, opposite party No. I failed to give even the date and time when the petitioner allegedly vacated the suit premises voluntarily making room for his entrance therein. None of the O.P.Ws except U.P.W. I himself, stated in his evidence that he saw the plaintiff petitioner leaving the suit premises voluntarily with the members of his family on taking away his belongings therefrom. Facts and circumstances of the case stand out prominently against the defence case of voluntary surrender of the suit property by petitioner Albert Subir Biswas in favour of opposite party No. 1 Abdur Rab Rashidi. The petitioner tiled T.S. No. 161 of 1995 before the learned Subordinate Judge. Dhaka for a decree of specific performance of a contract based on a written bainapatra. Opposite party No. 1 allegedly received about Tk. 8 lacs out of the total consideration of Tk. 9 lacs as earnest money. The petitioner is admittedly armed with an on order of status quo in respect of the suit property, which is virtually an order of injunction in his favour, he being admittedly in possession of the suit property at the relevant time. In such circumstances the story that the petitioner has voluntarily left the suit property in favour of opposite party No. 1 is certainly against the natural course of human behaviour and must therefore, be discarded as a fantastic story. The uncorroborated solitary statement of O.P.W. 1 on this point deserves no credence in the face of the most consistent, corroborative and overwhelming evidence or P.Ws. 1-4, well supported by an unbroken chain of circumstances convincingly proving the dare-devil manner in which the opposite parties at the behest of opposite party No. 1, under instant threat of life, drove away the petitioner and the members of his family from the suit property and illegally took over possession thereof in willful violation of the order of the Court. If there was any amount of truth in the defence plea that the petitioner voluntarily vacated the suit property, it was incumbent upon opposite party No. 1 to bring this important fact to the notice of the Court for evading the charge of violation of the order of the Court. 

 26. It may, in this connection, be mentioned that it has been stated in the written objection that the petitioner in the 2nd salish amicably handed over possession of the suit premises to opposite party No. 1 and left the same bag and baggage but there is absolutely no evidence on record to this effect. In view of the fact that opposite party No. 1 during trial of the Misc. Case could not adduce any evidence that the petitioner immediately after the 2nd salish handed over possession to him and voluntarily left the suit premises the case of the opposite parties in this regard appears to be a myth. 

 27. It may also be mentioned that the learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment opined that O.P.Ws. are disinterested and reliable witnesses. It is found from the record that the OPWs. 1, 2 and 3 are parties in the violation Misc. Case and the petitioner made repeated allegations of threat against them. 

 28. It may be mentioned that P.Ws. examined in the case are in some way or the other related to P.W.1 or are his employees or former employees but they are found to be natural and probable witnesses having no special reason to depose falsely in the case. In a case of this nature, it must be found that the PWs examined in the case are competent witnesses to prove the case of the petitioner as they are the best persons who would know of the act of forcible dispossession of the petitioner and the members of his family from the suit premises by the opposite parties in dis-obedience to the order of the court. There is no material discrepancy in the evidence of the P.Ws. and there is no earthly reason to disbelieve them. There is no denying the fact that the petitioner could not examine the neighbouring people in this case but P.W. 1 satisfactorily explained the position when he stated in his evidence that the opposite parties are men of dangerous and desperate character and as such the local people did not dare depose against the opposite parties for fear of life. This fact has been amply corroborated by the other PWs. 

 29. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record we are of the view that the O.P.W. 1 and his associates being armed with deadly weapons, entered into the suit premises on 19.3.96 and looted away furniture and other valuable properties from the suit premises forcibly evicted the petitioner and his men therefrom and took possession thereof willfully violating the order of status quo. There is no dispute about the fact that the petitioner was aware of the status quo order which was passed in his presence. It further appears from the record that the alleged voluntary abandonment of the suit premises by the petitioner and other inmates could not be proved by the opposite parties. The opposite parties rather asked the petitioner to vacate the premises within 48 hours in default of payment of rent and this clearly tantamount to violation of order of status quo passed by the Court. 

 31. None of the PWs examined in this case has stated that the other opposite parties except opposite party No. 1 was aware of the order of status quo while forcibly evicting the petitioner from the suit property on 19.3.96. In such view of the matter, it cannot be concluded with any amount of certainty that opposite party Nos. 2-7 willfully violated the order of the Court rendering them liable for willful disobedience of the order of the Court. Opposite party Nos. 2-7 are, therefore, entitled to get the benefit of doubt. But in so far as opposite party No. 1 is concerned, it has been proved by most consistent, corroborative and overwhelming evidence, both oral and documentary, that he forcibly evicted the petitioner from the suit property with the help of his associates on 19.3.96 in flagrant and willful violation of the order of status quo passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in respect of the suit property and as such he deserves punishment for such violation. 

 32. It is unfortunate that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court Dhaka failed to apply his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and consequently fell in error in passing the impugned order on a mis-reading and non-reading of the material evidence and non-consideration of vital facts and the material evidence. The reasoning’s and arguments advanced by the learned Subordinate Judge in support of his decision are found to be shockingly unreasonable bordering perversity and contrary to the evidence on record and as such the impugned order must be set aside in the interest of justice. 

 33. There is no dispute to the proposition of law that any order passed by a competent Court has a sancity of its own and it is binding upon all concerned under all circumstances unless set aside by a superior Court or by the Court itself by way of review on legal grounds. Any willful violation or disregard of the order of the Court is a matter of serious concern for the society and the wrong-doers must be adequately punished in accordance with law, otherwise the dignity of the Court and the majesty of law will be seriously impaired and the public confidence in the rule of law will be rudely shaken with dreadful consequences to follow. We are conscious that in dealing with a case of willful violation of its order, the court never acts with any amount of vengeance or arrogance but it draws a golden balance between the magnitude of the offence and the manner in which it has been perpetrated and the punishment to be meted out to the willful violators. In this case, it has been convincingly proved beyond doubt that opposite party No. 1 Abdur Rab Rashidi took the law in his own hands to forcibly evict petitioner Albert Suhir Biswas and the members of his family from the suit property on 19.3.96 defying all lawful efforts by the victim in obtaining an order of status quo from the learned Subordinate Judge, lodging repeated G.D. Entries at the Gulshan Thana and lastly filing a criminal case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. It has also been convincingly proved that in effecting the forcible eviction of the petitioner from the suit property opposite party No. 1 exhibited extreme high-handedness brutal ferocity and dreadful atrocity, with no regard for law. In the process opposite party No. 1 and his men caused heavy losses to the petitioner by illegally taking his valuable machinery and other articles worth lacs of taka. 

 35. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part with cost, which we assess at Tk. 2,500.00. The impugned order dated 17.1.95 passed in Misc. Case No. 161 of 1995 by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka in so far as it relates to opposite pity No.1 Abdur Rab Rashidi is hereby set aside. Opposite party No. 1 Abdur Rab Rashidi is found guilty of willful violation of the order of status quo, which has the affect of a prohibitory injunction, under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for forcibly evicting petitioner Albert Subir Biswas from the suit property on 19.3.96 in flagrant violation of the order of the Court and consequently it is ordered that opposite party No. I Abdur Rab Rashidi be detained in civil prison for a period of 3(three) months and properties worth taka thirty lacs belonging to him be attached for a period of one year for the time being. The order of attachment shall stand vacated as and when opposite party No. 1 Abdur Rab Rashidi restores possession of the suit property to petitioner Albert Subir Biswas as it stood on 19.3.1996.
